Gaming_Tech.title: UK also affected by cyber-attack which hit European fridges
Gaming_Tech.text:
Businesses in the UK's food supply chain have been impacted by the cyber-attack which hit supermarket fridges and freezers across Europe on Monday.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says it is aware of "a couple of instances where vulnerable technology had been exploited in the UK."

The NCSC's chief executive Dr Richard Horne told the Today programme, on BBC Radio Four, that it had "worked through the night" to alert potentially affected organisations in the UK.

The British Association of Independent Meat Suppliers (AIMS) told the BBC some of its more than 300 members had unexpectedly become what it called "collateral" as part of the hacks.

Two members saw their fridges begin to defrost, AIMS said, while another saw their cold units rise up to 100C (212F) in temperature.

AIMS spokesman Tony Goodger said the affected devices were empty at the time so no produce was lost - but urged businesses to be vigilant.

The incident "must act as a reminder to all in the food industry at whatever point in the supply chain they are that their businesses may be seen by some as targets," he said.

On Monday, supermarkets in countries including Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, and Belgium reported fridges and freezers being hiked in temperature.

The events followed attacks targeting supermarkets and food suppliers across France in early October.

Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Those attacks exploited vulnerabilities in some systems used to remotely control and manage cold refrigeration units that had been surfaced by cyber-security researchers months prior.

Horne told the BBC on Tuesday that it was still "too early to say" who was behind the hacks.

But he said it pointed to an urgent need for organisations and businesses to ensure the technology underpinning a whole range of applications we use and need daily was secure and up-to-date.

"That technology base we rely on as a society has not been invested on to the extent it needs to be," Horne said, noting many firms had extended systems beyond their end of life, not upgraded them nor kept them in secure compartments disconnected from the internet.

Such actions can create vulnerabilities that many cyber-security experts say amounts to low-hanging fruit for hackers, and can be easily exploited.

But the UK's cyber chief said that they could be found and exploited more quickly and easily via "AI in the hands of our adversaries".

"We do need all organisations to look at what they rely on, to invest in renewal," he said.

"We intervene where we can. But, at the end of the day, it's your business. It's your charity. It's your life. You need to make the choice and choose wisely."

Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected in Monday's cyber incident, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up.

The same method was thought to have been used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.

As with that incident, many of the retailers affected on Monday said they had no choice but to throw away spoiled food - some saying this amounted to hundreds of thousands of euro in lost produce.

Mathieu Tilman, who runs a Delhaize supermarket in Belgium, told the BBC he found it "truly distressing".

"There's so many people starving, people who don't have enough to eat. How can we end up throwing away so much food?"

"In moments like these, you just feel like quitting your job."

So far, there have been little to no signs of any such impact in the UK.

But the BBC has approached major UK supermarkets for comment and asked what action, if any, they are taking to safeguard against any similar hacks attempts.

"Retailers invest heavily in their cybersecurity and are currently working with the NCSC to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks," said Graham Wynn, assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.

Asda, Lidl, M&S, Sainsbury's and Tesco are among the retail trade association's members.

Paul Chichester, director of operations at the NCSC, said at the launch of its annual report on Tuesday it was continuing to work with and monitor UK organisations affected.

"At the moment, the impact is minimal," he added.

"We're working with organisations identifying existing vulnerabilities in the UK and trying to get those closed before somebody exploits them."

Gaming_Tech.title: Apple unsure when it will get more foldable iPhones ahead of Christmas
Gaming_Tech.text:
Apple has said it does not know when it will get more of its new foldable iPhones back in stock as the company heads towards the key Christmas trading period.

The iPhone Duo sold out just over a week after its launch, despite being Apple's most expensive smartphone at a cost of nearly $2,000.

The company warned of "constraints" in sourcing key components and admitted it was "really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance".

Meanwhile, Apple's new chief executive John Ternus said the firm was seeing an "unprecedented" price rise in memory costs, including chips, as the artificial intelligence (AI) industry continues to invest billions of dollars in building data centres.

Ternus launched the Duo after he took over from previous boss Tim Cook in September.

It is the smartphone's first major design change in almost 20 years but some buyers have reported problems with the Duo's screen.

Last week, the company said it would replace any handsets that were affected by an issue that caused a "small number" to crack along the inside fold.

As it released its latest financial figures on Monday, Apple's executives did not mention any problems with the iPhone Duo.

Ternus said he was "thrilled" by the early reaction to the foldable phone. Chief operating officer Sabih Khan said the company was working hard to get the Duo "into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible".

Apple's results for the three months to 26 September did not include sales of the Duo, which was released at the end of October.

Nevertheless, Apple said it had sold more iPhones globally over the last year than ever before.

iPhone revenue for the quarter rose 17% to $57bn (£42bn).

Sales of Mac computers also grew over the three months by 27% to a record $10.7bn.

Overall, Apple's sales between July and September rose from $102bn to $114bn. Pre-tax profit also increased, from $32.8bn to $36.1bn.

However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and watch, fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.

Khan said that most Apple devices were still experiencing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with advanced nodes.

Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allow Apple devices to operate more quickly, most of which it has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.

Khan said the problem was expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs.

The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.

Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of devices to store data like apps, photos and text messages.

Much memory storage runs through data centres, which have experienced a boom in demand for space as AI chatbots and platforms - including those developed by the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic - have become popular.

Gaming_Tech.title: North Korea denies being behind $6.3bn Binance crypto hack
Gaming_Tech.text:
North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".

Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.

This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.

Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.

The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.

"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.

"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.

But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.

The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.

Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.

The country has consistently denied such claims.

Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".

Gaming_Tech.title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.

Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.

And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.

However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.

Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.

But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.

Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.

"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.

He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.

"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.

Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.

The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.

However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.

That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.

The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.

Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.

It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.

When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.

Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.

Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.

"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.

He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.

"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.

"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."

Gaming_Tech.title: Binance hack: Users withdraw $3.6bn after record crypto heist
Gaming_Tech.text:
Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.

The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.

Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack.

The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.

Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."

There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.

Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.

The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack.

Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.

Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.

"We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme.

"The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added.

Gaming_Tech.title: Neoclouds: These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
Gaming_Tech.text:
A once-obscure corner of the AI ecosystem finds itself in the spotlight – and investors don't all like what they see.

Names like CoreWeave and Nebius are familiar to the tech set in San Francisco and Silicon Valley.

These data centre companies, known as neocloud firms, run large warehouses packed with expensive computers, which they lease to major AI developers like Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta.

They're now the subject of one of Silicon Valley's most heated debates.

Many question whether neocloud firms are financially sound and what their recent stumbles tell us about the state of the AI economy.

Analysts at Gartner predict by 2030, 80% of neocloud firms will "cease independent operations", while Forrester's experts expect at least three of them to be imminently acquired "as finances get shaky".

On Thursday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tried to downplay recent concerns about neocloud firms, calling them "a small component of the overall ecosystem, external" on CNBC.

Neocloud firms often finance themselves by signing long-term lease contracts with major tech customers who need quick access to computing power.

Firms can then borrow money using those contracts – plus the AI chips they purchase – as collateral, explained analyst Cory Johnson of "The Quiet Period" IPO research outfit.

He said debt is common across neocloud firms because the hardware has to be paid for up front.

Take the industry leader: CoreWeave. It's a fraction of the size of some of the Big Tech companies it serves.

But Johnson believes lenders sometimes consider the creditworthiness of CoreWeave's customers, like Microsoft or Meta, more than the company's when they lend.

"This helps explain how CoreWeave accumulated $35.1bn (£26.3bn) in debt," he said.

Some jittery investors appear to be having second thoughts.

CoreWeave stock has lost a quarter of its value over the past month, and it's not alone.

Shares in other neocloud firms like Nebius, IREN, and Applied Digital have all shed about that much if not more during the same period.

Debt investors also appear spooked, and are demanding ever-higher returns from several firms in the sector.

CoreWeave's CEO Mike Intrator has said that the market is acting "irrationally" and has expressed confidence in its business model. Some of the world's most consequential companies are queuing up for CoreWeave's infrastructure and other AI services.

Several neocloud firms have their roots in the volatile crypto mining industry, made of companies that generate cryptocurrencies, like Bitcoin.

Crypto miners use some of the same kind of physical infrastructure that is used to develop AI.

CoreWeave was founded in 2017 with a focus on mining Ethereum.

IREN, Core Scientific and Applied Digital also started in crypto mining.

Their infrastructure left them well-positioned when AI exploded in 2022 with the introduction of OpenAI's ChatGPT.

One outlier is Nebius, which was known as Yandex NV when it was part of Russia's version of Google before splitting off and changing its name in 2024.

Now, the success of these firms hinges on the fate of major AI developers and hyperscalers – even larger data centre operators which neocloud firms often count as key customers.

"There is just an enormous amount of spending getting injected into the system," said Melissa Otto, head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. "It's an arms race."

And neoclouds have benefitted.

But the trade-off of their model is "greater financial risk" in the face of change, said Forrester VP and principal analyst Charlie Dai.

That includes any adjustments that their Big Tech customers might make to their spending plans.

This past week, when Microsoft and Google forecast less AI spending than Wall Street analysts had projected, shares in several neocloud firms tumbled.

Much is also riding on Anthropic and OpenAI, which are both expected to start selling shares to the public in the months ahead.

If AI proves to be a bubble – and bursts – neocloud firms "are definitely going to face collateral damage," said Bradley Tusk of Tusk Ventures.

Gaming_Tech.title: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
Gaming_Tech.text:
Two major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.

The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.

This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.

Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.

Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim.

The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.

Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange.

In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency.

The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities".

The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports.

Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups.

Much of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain.

North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022.

In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker.

TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme.

Binance has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area.

Entertainment.title: Married at First Sight UK cancelled after BBC revealed rape allegations
Entertainment.text:
Married at First Sight UK will not return, Channel 4 has said, following a BBC investigation into the hit reality TV show.

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis earlier this year, after Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

A review was commissioned by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster, with details of the allegations we had heard.

On Thursday, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

The broadcaster's chief executive Priya Dogra said she was "very sorry for the distress those women have clearly felt", adding that the show's budget would be reinvested in "distinctive new programming".

The Panorama investigation in May, in which three women made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny, made the following allegations:

One woman said her onscreen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.

A second woman told both Channel 4 and CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her onscreen husband. Her episodes were still aired.

A third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - accused her onscreen husband of sexual misconduct.

All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.

Lawyers for CPL, the independent production company that makes the UK version of the show, previously said its welfare system is "gold standard" and industry-leading, and that it acted appropriately in all these cases.

Channel 4 had initially told Panorama that all the allegations were "wholly uncorroborated".

Dame Caroline Dinenage MP, chair of the House of Commons culture and media committee, said the decision to axe the show "makes sense" given the review's findings and the "seriousness of the allegations".

"Reality TV contestants have often been treated as a commodity, with duty of care a slogan rather than a genuine principle. Everyone involved in producing and regulating reality TV must now learn and act," she added.

A spokesman for Ofcom said the broadcast regulator would "carefully consider the reports published today as we move to strengthen our guidance for broadcasters".

"We are clear that broadcasters have a duty of care towards members of the public who participate in their programmes."

The review into the show was split into two - one part examined welfare protocols on MAFS UK, and the other reported on how Channel 4 handled the allegations.

The review into welfare protocols, led by former BBC One Controller Lorraine Heggessey, concluded that some parts of the programme's format increased "the risk profile of the show".

Although she found the protocols for MAFS UK were extremely thorough and of a high standard, she said "intimacy is a key focus", and that "some elements of the show could implicitly put pressure on contributors to be intimate".

Heggessey made suggestions including installing CCTV in all areas of the apartments, constantly monitored by a welfare team, with panic buttons and "safe words" in place.

She concluded that, with enhancements to the existing welfare framework and adjustments to the format, it would have been reasonable to continue to produce future series of MAFS UK.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme on Thursday, she added that the suggested changes "would have, in lots of ways, changed both the format and the nature of the show, but would have given the kind of protection that both Channel Four and CPL would have ideally looked for to ensure the safety of all contributors".

But she added that she "completely understood" why Dogra "decided that she doesn't want to proceed with it".

The other part of the review, by law firm Clyde & Co, found that Channel 4 and CPL's welfare protocols were compliant with Ofcom's broadcasting code.

There were no findings of a breach of the code regarding the handling of issues raised at the relevant times.

But it said there were "a small number of instances" where the show's protocols had not been fully applied.

This included one incident when "some contributors contravened the Code of Conduct relating to prohibited substances but were given a first and final warning rather than being removed from the programme".

It added that Channel 4 and CPL could have undertaken a more structured longer-term review over multiple series.

The review also made recommendations for areas where the contributor welfare framework could be "further strengthened".

Dogra said welfare across all of their programmes is "a primary concern".

She said that considering the "wholesale implementation" of the recommendations "provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over 10 years".

She added that the review "did not have the authority to adjudicate on the very serious allegations made by three women in the Panorama programme".

Billed as a "bold social experiment", Married at First Sight UK - known to many as MAFS - sees single people agree to "marry" total strangers, after meeting for the first time at their mock weddings.

The marriages are not legally binding, but viewers see the couples go on honeymoon, before moving in together and navigating their relationships - all while being filmed, almost every day.

The UK version, which had been running for 10 seasons, is one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.

Following the Panorama broadcast, Channel 4's chief executive Priya Dogra initially didn't apologise, although she did express her "sympathy" for those who had spoken up.

Less than 48 hours later, she changed position, telling reporters she was "deeply sorry" over the women's distress.

The impact of the Panorama progamme was swift, and sizeable.

Channel 4 launched its external review, all the episodes were taken down from its streaming service, and a major sponsor pulled out.

Married at First Sight UK usually starts airing in September, but the new series was put on hold following the revelations in the Panorama.

Ofcom has since launched an investigation, and in June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape.

The individual is not being named. The alleged victim is also not being named; anyone who makes an allegation of rape is entitled to anonymity by law.

If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

Entertainment.title: Sir Tom Jones tells fans he thought life 'was over' after flu
Entertainment.text:
Sir Tom Jones has told fans he feared his life was "over" after being admitted to hospital in the US with flu.

The 86-year-old from Pontypridd spent a week at the Ronald Regan UCLA Medical Center in Los Angeles and was forced to cancel or reschedule a number of concerts.

But on Wednesday night, he was back on stage at the Greek Theatre and told the audience just how serious his "bad case of the flu" was.

"[I thought] Oh well, this is it, you've had a wonderful life, Tommy, but it's over right now," he said.

"I must say this, in the UCLA, they really did a wonderful job. So I'm here."

"[The medical staff said] What do you want to do now? I was in there for a week. And I said, 'I've got to get back on the stage'. This is where I belong. I can't live without this, believe me."

Sir Tom recently made headlines after revealing ITV had "made the decision" to "fire" him from The Voice UK coaching panel, having served as an coach on the singing competition since its debut in 2012.

In the latest series, and his last as a coach, he mentored Welsh singer Cate McHugh to victory.

Entertainment.title: John Frieda: Celebrity hairstylist dies aged 75
Entertainment.text:
British celebrity hairstylist and beauty brand entrepreneur John Frieda has died aged 75.

Frieda became a firm favourite with celebrities throughout the 1960s and 1970s, and is known to have cut hair for clients including British model Twiggy, US First Lady Jackie Kennedy and Rolling Stones frontman Mick Jagger.

He was also known for the range of hair products bearing his name, and the iconic Purdey bowl cut which he created for The New Avengers actor Joanna Lumley in 1976.

His death was announced by his hair salon in an Instagram post on Tuesday., external

"It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our dear John passed away peacefully ….surrounded by his family", the statement said

"John was more than a mentor to us; he was a true icon of the hair industry. He was the person who taught us everything, believed in us, and made us better.

"Rest in peace, John. You will be forever in our hearts."

Throughout his career, Frieda worked with other famous clients including Diana, Princess of Wales, Madonna, Nicole Kidman and Scarlett Johansson.

Born Alan Howard Frieda in London in 1951, his father was a hairdresser who owned a salon in Ealing, west London, while his grandfather had also been a Fleet Street barber.

After having gone into the family business, Frieda later joined Leonard Lewis's star-studded salon House of Leonard - famous for having created Twiggy's famous crop - becoming his assistant.

He went on to work for fashion magazines British Vogue and Harper's Bazaar.

In 1976, Frieda opened his own salon in central London which became massively successful and booked up months in advance as his reputation as an influential stylist grew.

He subsequently opened branches across the world, including in Barbados, Ibiza and Los Angeles.

In the 1990s, Frieda stepped back from cutting hair and concentrated on developing his own brand of hair products, including Frizz-Ease hair serum which he created in 1988.

His business empire grew rapidly over the following decade as it expanded into the US and across the world.

In 2002, he and his business partner Gail Federici sold the company to a Japanese conglomerate Kao for $450m (£334m).

Speaking to the British Beauty Council, external in June, Frieda gave his advice for future generation of British hairdressers.

"If you have a client in front of you, rather than thinking about the money or what you're getting from cutting their hair, just think about the action," he said.

"The reward is giving her the best haircut she's ever had. That is your reward."

Model and TV personality Jo Wood, the ex-wife of Rolling Stones guitarist Ronnie Wood, described the news of his death as "so sad".

"When I was 16 and John worked as an assistant at Leonard's he would do my hair," she recalled. "He was so great..."

Cetera Lamb, creative director at Frieda's London salon said the industry had lost "a true legend, a real maverick in hairdressing".

"For 50 years, he led our wonderful salon, leaving behind an incredible legacy of passion, creativity, vision and outstanding hairdressing.

"We will continue in his honour, celebrating his achievements and keeping his memory, values, vision and love for great hairdressing alive. His legacy will live on through us, and we will make sure of that."

Entertainment.title: Quentin Tarantino and Kylie Minogue film movie in Porthcawl
Entertainment.text:
Sharing a pint with Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction director Quentin Tarantino in his local pub was a surreal experience for a Welsh filmmaker.

But this was just the tip of the iceberg for Jamie Adams, who also managed to get singing icon Kylie Minogue and rapper RZA from the Wu-Tang Clan to Porthcawl for his new movie.

The arrival of the stars in the seaside town earlier this year to work on Tangled Up in Blue caused a buzz, and Adams admitted it felt like "an out of body experience" bringing his heroes to his hometown.

It is not the first time he has brought big names to south Wales, having worked with Dirty Dancing star Jennifer Grey on 2019 film Bittersweet Symphony.

Adams was able to include scenes in locations that mean a lot to him, including the pub his dad used to run.

"It was called the Ship and Castle then and the bar is actually a boat that he brought from Weymouth, which is where I was born," he said.

"So I've got Quentin Tarantino having a pint with me in my dad's old pub, talking to Neil, one of my old pals, who I've known since I was like eight years old.

"It's all very surreal and beautiful."

Tangled Up in Blue follows a talent manager (Tarantino) who has spent 40 years managing legends but finds himself stranded at a hotel bar caught between an old flame and a lost soul.

It all fell into place with the involvement of the superstars after Adams filmed in France in 2025.

He shot a movie there in a week in his usual improv style - which is where much of it is created spontaneously rather than being read from a pre-written script.

Adams said Tarantino thoroughly enjoyed it, and described it as reminding him of French New Wave cinema that emerged from the late 1950s to the late 1960s.

"I said [to him] I'd love to do one that was a little bit more personal to me and actually shot in in my hometown," Adams added.

"He was very excited about coming.

"He'd never been to Wales before."

Getting Minogue, who has described herself as "half Welsh" to be part of the project was even easier.

Her family actually hail from near Porthcawl, with mum Carol Jones and her Welsh-speaking Nain, external Millie Jones emigrating from Maesteg, also in Bridgend county, to Australia in the 1950s.

Despite these strong roots in the country, she told Adams she was rarely able to visit, so jumped at the chance.

Adams said it felt right to do most of the filming in Wales' capital Cardiff and his hometown for what was such a personal movie.

He also loved the process of showing what his star cast was capable of but not necessarily known for.

Tarantino is better known for his work behind the camera, while Minogue has become one of the world's most famous pop stars after leaving Australian soap Neighbours in the late 1980s.

Adams also liked the fact his improv approach gave them freedom over their characters in a way that might not be possible on other productions.

While there is no current release date, the director is aiming for summer 2027.

He also hopes Cardiff can play host to a premiere, with his star cast attending.

"I think you've got to be very grateful that you were able to work with them," he added.

"It was about bringing a spirit a joy to south Wales."

Entertainment.title: Skewen pays tribute to Bonnie Tyler with new mural
Entertainment.text:
A mural of Bonnie Tyler has been unveiled in her hometown as a tribute to the global star "who never forgot her roots".

The Holding Out For a Hero singer, whose real name was Gaynor Hopkins, died in a hospital in Portugal in July, aged 75, after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery earlier this year.

Hundreds lined the streets of Skewen, in Neath Port Talbot, where she was born and raised, to pay their respects on the day of her funeral.

Artist Steve Jenkins, who painted the piece at Skewen Memorial Park, said it was "important" and the "pressure was on" to get the artwork right for the community.

The mural features a large picture of Tyler's face, as well as references to the local rugby club and Total Eclipse of the Heart - one of her best-known hits.

Speaking to BBC Wales, walkers passing the mural described the tribute as "fantastic".

Susan Petrosillo, 61, from Skewen, said she was "very, very proud".

"It's absolutely fantastic what they've done. It's such a lovely park as well," she said.

"She was such a big part of Skewen and still is."

For those who grew up alongside her, like Michael Davies, the mural is a chance to remember someone they knew long before she became a global superstar.

"I was in school with her, so I did know her quite well," he said.

"She was a Skewen girl, so it's tremendous."

Jenkins, known as Jenks Art, said the design evolved several times before reaching its final form.

"The first mock-up we had had Mumbles Lighthouse in the background," he said.

"But [with Tyler] being so proud of being from Skewen, we decided to put Skewen Park in the background."

He added the two-tone design of Tyler's face also carried a deeper meaning.

"As I was painting it, and as I was being approached by people, it became apparent that her music is going to live on.

"And that's sort of represented in the colour side of the face, and then, being a memorial piece, the black-and-white side of the face represents that."

Entertainment.title: Paul Chuckle prepares for stage debut at National Theatre
Entertainment.text:
They say it's never too late to try something new and, after more than six decades in the entertainment industry, Paul Chuckle is about to prove that true.

Real name Paul Elliott, the 79-year-old, is preparing to appear in his first ever play, taking on the role of Mr Boo in Jim Carwright's The Rise and Fall of Little Voice at the National Theatre.

Elliott, from Rotherham, became a household name, alongside his late brother Barry, as one half of the haphazard Chuckle Brothers in children's TV show ChuckleVision, which ran from 1987 to 2009.

But now, after decades of playing for laughs, he is just weeks away from what he has described as his first ever "straight play".

Speaking to the BBC, he said: "63 years in the business and it's my first ever play, and, would you believe it, it's at the National Theatre - you can't write it.

"A young lad from East Herringthorpe, and now at the National.

Following the death of his brother in 2018, Elliott said he was determined not to retire, and, in recent years, has turned his hand to a variety of new opportunities.

In 2025 he starred in a gangster movie, playing The Jackal in Fall to the Top, and later the same year appeared in Celebrity MasterChef.

In keeping with trying new things, he is also set to star as Monsignor O'Hara in a touring production of Sister Act at the end of 2027.

The Rise and Fall of Little Voice tells the story of as a shy girl who rarely ventures outside her bedroom, until her talent for imitating famous singers is recognised by a local promoter.

Elliott will perform alongside Silent Witness actress Francesca Mills, who will play the title role, and Waterloo Road star Jill Halfpenny, who will play her mother, Mari Hoff.

After a career including, TV, film, pantomime, circus and now regular DJ sets, he said adapting had been a challenge.

"It's completely different," he said.

"It's the first show I've done in many, many years without saying 'to me, to you'.

"The lines are slowly sinking into my brain.

"I've found that hard. Barry and I ad libbed a lot when we were on stage.

"We had lots of fun, we used to fall about laughing at each other, but there's none of that, I've got to be word perfect.

"TV is easier. If you go wrong it's 'cut, do it again' but on stage you can't.

"When me and Barry worked together we loved things going wrong, but you can't do that in a live play."

One thing Elliott said he did know well ahead of stepping into the shoes of club promoter Mr Boo was the world of working men's clubs.

"Jim Cartwright, who wrote the play, he thought I would be perfect for the part of Mr Boo," he said.

"I was working in working men's clubs all my career, and he knew I was doing that.

"We did all the clubs in the North East, South Wales, Midlands, North Wales, wherever we could get the work, we grew up in working men's clubs. Not an easy life, may I tell you. Not an easy life.

"You never knew whether they're going to love you or hate you, and there was no real middle ground.

"They were either a fabulous audience or a terrible audience, or put it the other way, we were terrible or brilliant."

Entertainment.title: ‘George Lucas told me off for wearing lipstick’: Celia Imrie on Traitors, Star Wars and treating the lens like a lover
Entertainment.text:
You looked as if you had such a good time on Celebrity Traitors last year – you had them hanging on your every word. What was it like? Who have you kept in touch with? breezehillpete

They absolutely didn’t hang on my every word. I’m fascinated to watch it now, because at a distance, I can see how people follow each other. That herd mentality is very evident at the round table, but I always went in a different direction and people didn’t follow me. Then, of course, I accused Alan [Carr] at the end: “I think you are one, aren’t you?”, so I had to go the next day. I didn’t quite know what I was letting myself in for, but I had a great time.

Kate [Garraway] and I had to go on that Uncloaked thing after. She turned to me and she said: “Oh, but Celia, we’re now all one big happy family, aren’t we?” I said: “Well, frankly, I don’t want to see any of them ever again in the whole of my life,” and everybody laughed. But truthfully, we haven’t really run into each other since. Nevertheless, I think I was with a marvellous company, and I liked them all.

You appeared to be most attentive during the 1987BBC Michael Caine Acting in Film class, which is now something of a hit on YouTube. He seemed to be a really generous and informed tutor. What techniques did you learn that you’ve taken with you? PaulyVLondon

Maria Aitken asked me if I’d like to take part. Some of my friends said: “Oh God, you don’t want to look like a student on television.” I said: “What are you talking about? I’d like to be able to say good morning the way Michael Caine does on film.” I was thrilled to be part of it. One of his famous things was: don’t blink in a closeup. He also said to work out any props the night before, and something rather marvellous: that you have to think of the camera as your lover. The camera is ready to love you, so you must reciprocate. I’ve remembered all of that.

So I sit down to watch Star Wars: The Phantom Menace and who do I see flying a spaceship? How on earth did you end up doing that? Bisleys_Jaffa_Cakes

Bizarrely, I was doing a play called The Hothouse with the late, great Harold Pinter. One matinee, little did I know that the casting director for Star Wars was sitting in the audience. She took one look at me in my nightie and thought: “She’d make a marvellous fighter pilot.” And I’m absolutely delighted that I became Bravo 5.

By the way, I have no idea whether I got shot down, whether I killed anybody, whether I survived or whose side I was on. I have absolutely no idea, except that I was Bravo 5. I got told off by George Lucas for wearing lipstick because I was the only girl – the only female fighter pilot.

What has been your experience of Hollywood? Too many weird offers, or have you just not been keen to spend the time there? nivlek47

No, I absolutely adore Hollywood. I spent five very, very happy seasons doing Better Things. I didn’t get any weird offers, funnily enough. I love Hollywood, everything about it, and I’d go back at the click of a finger.

Did your son, Angus Imrie, who has played Josh Archer since 2014, ever let slip any spoilers from The Archers? And if so, did you keep the secret? JamesMoriarty

I’ve just spoken to my son, funnily enough, who is filming in San Francisco. And he was quite amused by the question and my answer, because my answer is: “No, he didn’t,” because I never listened to it. Some loyal mother am I.

I used to live in the same block as you in south London. Were you in to hear the cheer echoing around the courtyard the night The Gathering Storm was on TV, when you made your first entrance as Churchill’s secretary, Violet Pearman, opposite Albert Finney as Churchill? Kalundborg

It’s a terribly sweet idea that people cheer when I come on the television. I was completely thrilled to be Churchill’s secretary with Albert Finney. It was a small part, but I used to come in every morning and say: “Actually, I’ve got an idea,” put it on his desk, and he’d say: “Oh, not another bloody idea,” which made me roar. But honestly, life’s not like that. I don’t remember being cheered, I’m sorry, but it’s a lovely idea.

Which painting do you covet? I ask because you briefly stood next to me at the Van Gogh exhibition at Tate Britain in 2019. i7777i

My favourite paintings are Monet’s paintings of the River Thames, which are completely breathtaking. There is another artist called André Derain, who produced a very colourful painting called Barges on the Thames. I would love to have that.

What was it like playing Edina’s PR archrival, Claudia Bing, in Absolutely Fabulous? Was the name a nod to Crystal Bing, who my mum knew and remembers referring to you as “dear Celia” in a very grand, Lady Bracknell-type voice. Fposte

Of course, I absolutely adored playing the archrival of Jennifer Saunders – who wouldn’t? It’s such a marvellous series. Especially because everybody understands greed and overindulgence, so it appeals to us all, doesn’t it? I got to wear some marvellous clothes as well, so I was rather thrilled to be part of it.

I did have a relation called Crystal Bing. I think she might have been a second cousin or something. When I first went to Los Angeles to film Calendar Girls, I got into the lift and this gentleman turned to me and said: “Oh, Claudia Bing – bing and bing,” and then pressed the “bing” on the lift and we went up together. He was the first person to recognise me in America.

What continues to inspire you to take on such varied work when you could simply be enjoying yourself? orangekeeps

When you say “take on such varied work when you could be simply enjoying yourself” – enjoying what? Simply enjoying myself doing nothing? If that’s the alternative, absolutely not. I love keeping people second-guessing, because I don’t want to be caught doing the same thing. I want to keep on switching things up and challenging myself and making the most of – without being dramatic – what time I’ve got ahead. I loved playing the barrister in War, because it took me to watch real cases at Southwark crown court. I can’t really be a Bond girl, but I wouldn’t mind being a Bond villain. I had trapeze lessons for [the film] Love Sarah, because Mimi was part of the circus. I can’t go particularly high, but I used to be a chorus girl, so I’ve got a bit of dance up my sleeve and can do a bit of a twirl.

Entertainment.title: Full of life and catching feelings: Christine and the Queens’ greatest songs – ranked!
Entertainment.text:
20. Forgive 8888888 (2024)

Originally leaked online by the artist himself, Christine and the Queens’ fifth album, Hopecore, was released under a new name of Rahim Redcar (he’s now back to releasing as Christine and the Queens, and using Chris as his own name). Hopecore eschewed the sophisticated pop of his early years in favour of lo-fi, roughly drawn sonic sketches, and this flighty opener is built around ricocheting drum beat patterns that are eventually pierced wide open by laser-like synths.

19. Je te vois enfin (2022)

Upset at his label, grieving his mother and heartbroken, he released a third album, Redcar les adorables étoiles (prologue), that was saturated in sadness. Created in a two-week burst, the songs often felt undercooked, or missing crucial elements – such as choruses – but the suave Je te vois enfin is a clear highlight, all slinky 80s synth-pop strutting.

18. Girlfriend (ft Dām-Funk) (2018)

If 2014’s breakthrough debut album, Chaleur humaine, was slow-burning, tactile and warm, then its taut Michael Jackson-influenced follow-up, Chris, was immediate, muscular and sweaty. On this lead single, featuring US funk experimentalist Dām-Funk, Chris playfully grapples with gender norms over Chic-esque guitar riffs and a finger-snap beat.

17. Deep Holes (2024)

“I never had this faith in me / That I could be that man” – so opens Hopecore’s poppiest moment, which, given it lyrically explores sexuality and gender identity over a relentless trance beat, is all relative. That it’s strangely thrilling – the “fefefafa” closing mantra sounds like an incantation – says a lot about Chris’s ability to surprise.

16. Narcissus Is Back (2011)

Chaleur humaine’s brilliance was how it refracted typical pop subject matters – love, heartbreak, loneliness – through a more rarefied lens. On Narcissus Is Back, which uses a rib-rattling bass thump as its core, a soon-to-be-ex is placed within the context of the Greek myth of its title: a man so obsessed with his image that he kisses himself.

15. Mura Masa – Second 2 None (ft Christine and the Queens) (2017)

On this low-key highlight of producer Mura Masa’s guest-stuffed debut album, Chris weaves the various shades of his voice through burbling steel pan flourishes and sudden snatches of breakbeat. Lyrically, it’s brutally direct in its exploration of a relationship built on a trust that is steadily disintegrating.

14. What’s-her-face (2018)

As Christine and the Queens, Chris’s outsiderhood comes baked in, with that moniker a reference to the drag queens that offered him solace. On this slow-moving track, the isolation is laid bare, but with each “ever ever” in the song’s coda there’s also a feeling of exorcising demons by staring them full in the face.

13. A Day in the Water (2023)

Inspired by crippling grief and Tony Kushner’s epic 1991 play Angels in America, Chris created the sonic equivalent of mausoleums on 2023’s epic, Madonna-assisted Paranoïa, Angels, True Love. A Day in the Water shimmers like mist on a lake as Chris offers himself up to a bigger entity, away from trouble bubbling elsewhere.

12. The Walker (2018)

As with What’s-her-face, Chris explores alienation and otherness on The Walker. He juts out his chin at people staring and immediately recognises the polite, don’t-come-any-closer smile of confused strangers. The occasionally brutal lyrics sit in contrast to the music, which accentuates the lovely central melody with 80s drums and synth filigrees.

11. Cerrone & Christine and the Queens – Catching Feelings (2025)

As undeniably interesting as it can be to hear Chris excavate his innermost demons over increasingly knotty soundscapes, there’s something thrilling about the directness of this collaboration with French disco pioneer Cerrone. Taken from their 2025 EP of the same name, Catching Feelings features Chris singing the word “dickheads” over a perfect reconstruction of a lost early-80s pop smash.

10. Jonathan (ft Perfume Genius) (2015)

Originally released in France in 2014, Chaleur humaine was repackaged the following year with a tweaked track listing that included this new track. Inspired by shame, beauty and Klaus Nomi, it’s a beautiful, bruised ballad, with Mike Hadreas’s emotionally swollen vocal bolstered by a quivering string section and Chris’s wordless coda.

9. To Be Honest (2023)

Chris wrestles with his recent past on his version of a blown-out 80s power ballad. “It is like a movie played by another star / She’s a stranger to be honest”, he sings, referencing his gender transition and the fallout from his sudden fame. The musical backdrop accentuates the drama, as billowing synth chords and OTT guitar riffs crash around him.

8. Doesn’t Matter (2018)

Written during a period of intense loneliness, the galloping Doesn’t Matter charts a journey of sorts. With a head full of dark characters (“the unravelled ones with their hands laying bare”) and thoughts of suicide, by the song’s end Chris reaches for joy, imploring those that have found light to hold on to it. As with all of Chris’s best songs, the thematic complexity is welded to pop brilliance.

7. Paradis perdus (2014)

Another example of crafting pop perfection from surprising source material arrives in the shape of Paradis perdus. While the verses are taken from Christophe’s Jean-Michel Jarre-produced French-language 1973 song, its chorus interpolates Kanye West’s 2008 single Heartless. The melancholy of the verses, in which a faded star is mourned, pairs perfectly with the grandiose sadness of West’s “coldest story ever told”.

6. I Disappear in Your Arms (2020)

Released in February 2020, a few weeks before global lockdown, the heartbroken La vita nuova EP took Chris’s nimble physicality and gave it a dead arm. Pierced through with a chunky synth bass, and peppered with snatches of vocal cries, this menacing bop addresses a selfish lover who wants something that doesn’t exist.

5. 5 Dollars (2018)

Inspired by the stripped back melodies of Bruce Springsteen, and Arthur Russell’s mix of sad-happy, 5 Dollars explores the complicated relationship between artist and consumer: the kind of love money can buy. As with most of second album Chris, the music is taut and sinewy, but there’s a lovely rush of fresh air that arrives with the song’s skyrocketing chorus.

4. Charli xcx & Christine and the Queens – Gone (2019)

Charli and Chris fuse their respective sounds – brash, metallic agitpop and decadent, undulating funk – on this hip-shaking ode to crippling anxiety. While Charli creates a horrific wall of mirrors in her verse, Chris leans into full-blown paranoia, all beady eyes staring and shadowy whisperings. The tension breaks somewhat on the chorus, but the whole thing sounds like two people hammering their way out of a metal box.

3. Full of Life (2023)

Built around Johann Pachelbel’s baroque bop Canon in D, and inspired by Björk, the monumental Full of Life grapples once more with grief, but this time its foundations are solidified by the vitality that can come through great loss. Recorded as if standing in the middle of a cathedral, Chris’s voice soars and sweeps, often in tandem with the sighing strings.

The song that changed everything for Christine and the Queens when he performed it at a rain-soaked, post-Brexit-vote Glastonbury in 2016. A soothing balm celebrating difference, eccentricity and warding against homogenisation, it seemed like the perfect island of hope to cling to. There’s something brilliantly simplistic about its chorus’s mantra: “I am actually good / Can’t help it if we’re tilted”.

1. People, I’ve Been Sad (2020)

Scalpel-sharp in its emotional brutality and yet somehow featherlight, People, I’ve Been Sad is Christine and the Queens in excelsis. Released just before Covid struck, sending everyone into their own private well of sadness, it favours introspection over wallowing. Regret, familial trauma and isolation are thus transformed into a beautiful confessional. Musically, its glowing synths, slow-burn pace and empathetic string section create a kind of luxuriant sadness that feels transportive.

Entertainment.title: Is that an explosion, an implosion or an orgasm? Pixies bass-player Emma Richardson’s realm-leaping life in painting
Entertainment.text:
Emma Richardson loves to eavesdrop when people look at her paintings and talk about what they see in them. “They turn into these Rorschach inkblot tests,” she grins. Looking at her works, you do stand back in awe wondering. Is that a nebula, a god or a fleshy, baroque orgy? An explosion, an implosion or an orgasm? Richardson implies all of these and more, her paintbrush chasing in vivid oils the hedonism, desire and breadth of human experience.

This fascination with the transcendent has in part been informed by her other life as a musician, formerly in the garage-rock trio Band of Skulls and currently playing bass and singing in Pixies.

“Teabag in or out?” she asks brightly, her studio flooded with natural light, illuminating her canvases, some two metres tall. We are in the far, ungentrified reaches of east London, where a Dickensian-vibes building with a glazed roof and bathroom tiles of architectural salvage dreams can still serve as affordable studios. It’s a muggy afternoon and some of the works remain bubble-wrapped after returning from Richardson’s home town: Southampton City Art Gallery recently underwent a £2m revamp and she was chosen for its grand reopening exhibition, Levitate Me: Desire, Ecstasy and the Sublime. “They did such an incredible job,” she says. “It was celestial.”

But the paintings won’t sit here long and nor will she: these works are destined for a new show across town, while their creator will soon be touring the US with Pixies. While Richardson’s degree was in painting, she has always made music. She was asked to join Pixies in 2024, having had a few years off performing to concentrate on painting. She left Band of Skulls during the pandemic, five albums in. “That experience of playing live definitely feeds into my work,” she says. “There’s an electricity in that connection between audience and performers, then the danger and fear – no one knows what’s going to happen next.”

This is especially true with Pixies because there is never a set list. The next song is always decided on the spur of the moment by Black Francis, lead singer and guitarist. “It’s a real thrill,” she says, “and the show goes so quickly because of that excitement. There’s an element of extreme focus, but you let loose as well. It’s really freeing.”

So she explores these experiences on canvas, “and other ways human beings choose to transcend. It’s fascinating to me how we choose to do that through dancing and raves and festivals, big sporting events, but also solitary meditation and connecting to ourselves a bit more deeply.”

Sex is a big one: “Those ecstatic peak experiences. I’m fascinated by desire and female sexuality, connection with other human beings, and the sublime in the natural world. We see it these days more and more with climate change and the storms and this uncontrollable nature. It’s the contemporary sublime, terror mixed with awe, but it’s all under this umbrella of ways of transcending.” Equally for some, this may involve “intoxication and psychedelics or it could be reading a book and getting lost in it.”

Richardson has a crate of her favourite books right here, fresh from being displayed alongside her exhibition in Southampton. Many focus on female desire, a subject she’s been doubling down on as she enters midlife at 44. Miranda July’s All Fours from 2024, Nell Dunn’s Talking to Women from 1964: “Lots of psychology of desire.” She mentions Audre Lorde’s Your Silence Will Not Protect You, which contains her famous 1978 essay about “the erotic as an inner, driving force, a life force, rather than the pornographic reading of the erotic. That fascinates me. That inner drive and push in women, trusting what brings you joy and what gives you pleasure. What do you want out of life? It’s important to figure out these things.”

There’s Gillian Anderson’s Want, too, the first of two collections of anonymously submitted sexual fantasies from women around the world. Richardson digs out another from the box. “This is an incredible book, Alphabetical Diaries by Sheila Heti. She put every single line of her diary into a spreadsheet and then ordered them alphabetically, but they link and make patterns. It’s brilliant when you get to I – and I am and I love and I hate. I’m intrigued by how other writers or artists or musicians explore what it is to exist in a female body.”

I spot the catalogue from the British surrealist painter Ithell Colquhoun’s 2025 exhibition at Tate Britain, a show that made me feel so seen as a red-blooded woman that I developed a palpable swagger the further I got around it. And a book on Artemisia Gentileschi, “one of the earliest baroque painters”, says Richardson. “She was very sassy and clever about how she painted her self-portrait, using powder pigments and oil.” Part of the power of Richardson’s work is that it’s steeped in the history of art – you can see abstract ghosts of Gentileschi, Rubens and the female surrealists – but takes the discourse somewhere new and peculiar to her.

She’s inspired visually, too, by the Hubble telescope and sci-fi films such as 2001: A Space Odyssey. “There’s a stargate sequence where they’re travelling through time. It’s like loads of flashing, colourful lights going past the helmet of the person in the spacecraft and the energy and colour feels like you’re lifting out of your body – that inspired a painting called I Slipped My Body Completely, which is that sensation that you’re hanging in space, this idea of a transitional state almost.” How to capture that statically in paint is the challenge, she says: “Surprising yourself with what comes out and what you can then work into further. It’s like hunting it down.”

When she talks about oil paints her eyes widen like a toddler investigating its first snail after a downpour. “It’s quite alchemic,” she says. “You can layer it, and you can make it glow and sing like no other medium. There’s something about the consistency, colour and depth you can create, the fact it stays wet so you can work into it and blur and smudge and mix.”

With canvases of this scale, she says, the work “envelops you, it’s wider than your vista”. But while on tour, she paints and draws in more portable dimensions, packing acrylic paint, charcoal and watercolour. “I work in hotel rooms and backstage and make small pieces. I need that outlet on tour.”

It has been 13 years, and two other bass players, since Pixies’ revered original bassist, Kim Deal, left. How has it felt taking on her mantle? “It’s huge shoes to fill and I’ve got nothing but respect for her,” says Richardson, “but all I can do is my best – and know they asked me to do it. But my voice does sound different, and I might have a different playing style. I can’t imitate, but respect.”

She plays the songs how they should be played, “but there’s going to be an element of myself in there. I hope that works with the current lineup. They seem happy, so I’m happy. But it’s an incredible position. And the basslines are so cool.” In fact, learning the songs was a revelation, as a longtime fan. “You realise how cleverly structured they are. They’re really tricky. The time signatures are quite different. There are sections you don’t expect cropping up, and not many repeats.” Richardson played on their 2025 album The Night the Zombies Came. “We’re looking to do some more recording, but it’s all very relaxed.”

The new London show is at the Wolf Collective – a commercial gallery within the curator’s Primrose Hill home. It’s called Hotwire My Heart, borrowed from a 1976 song by a band called Crime, later covered by Sonic Youth. “It has a real frenzied garage rock’n’roll sound like the Stooges,” she says. “I heard it back when I was at Wimbledon School of Art, loved it and titled one of my degree show paintings with the name.” Hotwire was also a name she used when she played solo gigs around Southampton when she was starting out. It feels apt, she says, to reuse the title for these paintings crystallising “the need to be whipped up into another realm”.

Entertainment.title: ‘Children were wearing fake life jackets’: one Syrian family’s terrifying, 10-year journey
Entertainment.text:
In 2015, an 11-year-old Syrian girl called Israa matter-of-factly explained how her family would survive if their dinghy sank crossing the sea from Turkey to Greece. Her father would grab her disabled sister; her mother would look after the baby. “And I,” said Israa, a huge smile lighting her face, “I know how to rescue myself.”

Wife-and-husband documentary-makers Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes met Israa while filming a BBC series, Exodus, about refugees trying to reach Europe. Their plan was to follow Israa and her family on their hazardous journey to Germany. But after Israa reached safety, the pair kept filming. Ten years in the making, their documentary, One in a Million, is extraordinary - with echoes of Richard Linklater’s Boyhood and the Up! series. We watch Israa grow up in front of our eyes, from a sunny-natured 11-year-old to a woman, married with a baby of her own.

Azzam and MacInnes first spotted Israa in İzmir, on the Turkish coast, selling cigarettes with her father to raise money to pay the people-smugglers. “This ray of sunshine appeared in front of us,” remembers Azzam, who is also Syrian. “Israa was smiling and started talking to us. It was love at first sight. She was so bubbly, enthusiastic and positive. We were talking to her, then her father. They invited us back to their flat.” The family had fled Aleppo after their home was destroyed by a missile.

Eleven-year-old Israa joked about the dinghy sinking, too young to understand the risks. But her father Tarek agonised: “I’m gambling with the lives of my children,” he says in the documentary. Just a few months earlier, the body of the three-year-old Syrian boy Alan Kurdi washed ashore in Turkey. The image was in Tarek’s mind as he parted from the film-makers on the night of the crossing: “If anything bad happens to us, you have to tell our story.”

McInnes still finds the scene emotional to watch: “At the time we knew there was a chance that we would say goodbye to them, and that would be it.”

Sitting next to him in the restaurant of a London hotel, Azzam brushes aways tears as she remembers filming in İzmir, a hub for the people-smuggling trade. “It was absolutely heartbreaking. You saw lots of families putting life jackets on their children.” McInnes adds: “People were selling fake life jackets as well. Life jackets that didn’t actually work. I’m not sure we could have filmed it if we’d had children at that point.”

The couple met in 2010 while working together. Soon after, McInnes relocated to Damascus where they planned to start a production company. When the Syrian uprising began in 2011, they moved to London, where they now live with their six-year-old son.

In 2015, after Israa’s family landed in Greece on the dinghy, they joined the flow of refugees. It was Europe’s biggest movement of people since the second world war. Israa trudged through mud and freezing rain carrying her baby brother, while her parents pushed her sister in a wheelchair. Azzam and McInnes were there every step of the journey. “We slept in the street with them. We went on refugee trains and buses,” says McInnes. “By the time we arrived in Germany, we just became a family.”

The family’s journey ended in Cologne, where they settled. But the film-makers found it impossible to walk away. Partly it was about the relationship they had built, explains Azzam: “When we got to Germany, Israa was asking: ‘Are you going to visit us?’ We said: ‘Of course.’”

It also didn’t feel like the end of the story, she adds: “When we started, the idea was: let’s document this journey. Then there was a lot of talk about integration: will these people integrate in Europe? So we kept filming to cover that. Then it became a film about a family and love. Part of the emotional rollercoaster of making this film was that it’s about everything.”

In Cologne, Israa learned fluent German in five months flat. She started school, made friends and fell in love with Justin Bieber. Aged 12, she chose not to wear the hijab, a decision she later revisited. Her once close relationship with her father became antagonistic. One in a Million is a portrait of the refugee crisis, but it’s also a coming-of-age story, a tale about growing pains that feels universal in places.

It took Izzam and McInnes three years to get any kind of financial backing. They juggled full-time jobs, whacking the cost of making the documentary on to credit cards. How bad did it get? “I think we were at least 40 grand in debt at a one point,” McInnes replies grinning. “But we were young freelancers.”

In the documentary, we watch the tectonic plates in the family’s dynamics begin to move. When he left Syria, Tarek lost much of his identity. In Aleppo he ran a falafel restaurant: “He was a big character there,” says McInnes. “Everyone knew him. Now here he is in Germany, just another immigrant.”

While Tarek struggled to adjust, the women in his life blossomed. Halfway through the film his wife Nisreen – Israa’s mother – a background figure at the start, steps in front of the camera. Her transformation is one of the joys of the film. “She has a sort of hero’s journey, doesn’t she?” says MacInnes. “It’s so wonderful to see what’s happened to her.”

When Israa was 14, she disclosed to MacInnes that her father had been hitting her, while they were out picking up kebabs. He switched off the camera and into safeguarding mode: “We suddenly realised something much more important was happening than the film,” he remembers. With great sensitivity the film-makers chronicled what happened next in the family.

Their plan was to stop filming when Israa reached 18. But then she met her future husband Mohammed, who also arrived in Germany from Syria as a child refugee. In late 2024, the Assad regime unexpectedly fell. The film is bookended with moving footage of Israa returning to Aleppo to visit.

For those of us who have never experienced being a refugee, the film is a powerful insight into what it might feel like to have to leave your country and the longing for home. Azzam nods: “I went through that. It’s a struggle. Even though I’m settled in the UK and we have a child together and our life is here, there’s something missing. You feel like a guest that overstayed their welcome. And you struggle with identity. Who am I? Am I Syrian? Am I British?” She shrugs as if to say an answer is impossible.

Does anti-immigrant, anti-refugee feeling in the UK upset her? “It is hard, but you get used to it. There’s a lot of negativity, and you learn to block it.” The rhetoric is also a million miles from her her day-to-day life. “I’ve been in this country for 14 years, and I have never experienced any racism. I understand that people have. But honestly, it’s been an absolutely positive experience. And my parents have been here for a year. They are absolutely shocked at how nice people are. They don’t speak English, and when they walk down the street, everyone smiles at them, tries to help them.”

Azzam is from the Druze religious minority in Syria. Months after the fall of the Assad regime, armed tribes reportedly backed by the new government clashed with Druze fighters in southern Syria. Her village was destroyed: “we saw footage of our house, completely black, burned down.” Her parents have been in London for a year and a half.

Back to the film, Azzam admits there were times when they felt they would never finish it: “Honestly, it was really intense to make. It was just out of passion really that carried on for so long.”

She exchanges a glance with MacInnes. He adds: “I remember when Israa was first in Germany, we used to push her on the swings. Now we push our kids together on the swings.”

Over a video call, I speak to Israa, sitting in the kitchen of her home outside Cologne. She smiles easily and often. Now in her early 20s, with two small children, she has returned to education and is training to be a civil servant in local government.

Does she remember meeting the film-makers? “Yes!” she says with one of her biggest, brightest smiles. “I felt a blind trust from the moment I saw Itab, I trusted her straight away. And our relationship over the years turned into a really deep friendship.”

The first time she watched One in a Million, she cried all the way through, she says. How did it feel watching scenes of her family prepare to make the crossing from Turkey? “As a child I wasn’t really aware how dangerous it was. But now, when I remember, when I watch the movie, I can see it was a really dangerous trip.”

I ask if becoming a mother has changed how she feels about the trek she took so young? She nods. “I always say that both of my parents are very brave. Because now as a mother when I look at my children, I say that I would never have the courage to do to take such a trip. I am very proud of them because they took this decision and went on this journey with us.”
